LangGraph is a legitimate piece of workflow software and not a wrapper framework, unlike other LangChain abstractions. It's a Pregel/BSP-based orchestration for cycles and parallelism without data races; can design your graph as a state machine.

Main thing LangGraph adds is a state machine framework for human-in-the-loop with time travel, e.g. letting an analyst fix LLM output at a step, try alternatives, and go back without building your own state machine.

A node in LangGraph doesn't have to be an agent, it can be any state manipulation function, giving flexibility to build preprocessing/postprocessing nodes; though it's odd there's no default Node class.
Wish persistence and streaming were better developed - they give sample code to stream, but it's essentially a complete implementation of streaming that every client needs to implement themselves.
Question raised: how can one deploy LangGraph as an API with production-like features beyond running langgraph serve locally?

Criticism: LangGraph introduces abstractions that are 'not properly documented or well maintained,' with frequent breaking changes, making the author skeptical of adopting it as a useful agentic framework.

You don't have to use langchain tools or ToolNode with LangGraph—nodes are just functions that can do whatever you want; scheduling, checkpointing, and state management are core LangGraph framework features, while tool abstractions are optional LangChain add-ons.

Hot take from framework comparison: built-in parallelism in LangGraph, while promising, can complicate debugging a lot; framework abstractions can add unnecessary complexity for experienced developers but may offer useful structure for less experienced teams.

Skeptical take: predeclaring a graph structure (as LangGraph/Pregel does) is an abnormal way of writing programs; if you want to dynamically change control flow, you'll wrestle against the up-front graph structure. Prefers writing normal-looking code without predeclared execution graphs.

Perceived benefits of LangGraph's Pregel-like graph approach: predeclaring structure enables full-graph debugging UI even for partially executed runs, and easier reasoning about global state transitions.

Almost none of those things are part of the LangGraph framework? LangGraph does the scheduling, checkpointing, state management, etc. All of those things are LangChain abstractions that you can use when building a graph.
Hot take #1: For experienced developers, framework abstractions can add unnecessary complexity. Hot take #2: Built-in parallelism, while promising, can complicate debugging a lot.

The one thing I wish was better developed is persistence and streaming - they give sample code to stream, but it's essentially a complete implementation of streaming that every client needs to implement.
